pos: pron. (second person singular, nominative; rendering Hebrew 'attah, Greek su)
etymology: From Saxon þu, cognate with Latin tu, Greek su, Hebrew 'attah. The Authorized Version keeps the old English singular where modern versions have flattened everything into you. Thou is not elevated speech; it is exact speech — it means one person and not two.
biblical_def: Thou is the second person singular of the Authorized Version, and it carries information that modern English has thrown away. Hebrew and Greek both distinguish the one from the many, and the KJV translators preserved that distinction in English: thou, thee, thy, thine for one person; ye, you, your, yours for more than one. The doctrinal weight of this is not small. The Decalogue reads “Thou shalt have no other gods before me” (Exodus 20:3) — singular, so that no Israelite could hide inside the congregation and treat the commandment as addressed to the nation in bulk. God calls the fallen man out from the trees by the singular: “Where art thou?” (Genesis 3:9). Christ finds all three disciples sleeping in the garden and rebukes one by name: “Simon, sleepest thou?” And Peter's confession is singular on both sides — “Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matthew 16:16). Every commandment, every promise, and every summons in the singular lands on a particular person who must answer for himself. The pronoun is a doctrine of personal accountability built into the grammar.
webster_summary: The second person singular pronoun, nominative case; used of one person only, as distinguished from ye and you, which are plural. In Scripture it marks the commandment, the promise, and the summons as addressed to a particular person rather than to a congregation in the mass.
webster_full: THOU, pron. [Sax. þu; L. tu; Gr. su.] The second personal pronoun, in the singular number; the nominative case.
2. It is used only in addressing a single person, and is opposed to ye and you, which are plural.
3. In common English discourse it has become disused, and you is substituted for the singular as well as the plural; but thou is retained in the solemn style, and in address to God.
4. THOU, v.t. To treat with familiarity; to address as thou.
5. In Scripture, Thou shalt have no other gods before me, Exo. 20; Where art thou? Gen. 3; Thou art the Christ, Matt. 16.
corruption_summary: The common notion that thou is stately, formal, God-only language has the truth exactly backwards: it is the plain, familiar, singular form. What is genuinely lost when it goes is not reverence but precision — the ability to tell whether Scripture is speaking to one soul or to a whole church.
corruption_paragraphs: The living misuse is a well-meaning one. Because thou survives in English chiefly in prayer and in the Authorized Version, readers infer that it must be an honorific — a special reverential register reserved for addressing God. Historically it is the opposite. Thou was the ordinary, intimate, singular address used between equals, to children, and to servants; you was the deferential plural borrowed for polite address to a superior. The KJV therefore has God addressed as Thou not because the pronoun is grand, but because there is one God and the worshipper speaks to Him directly. To read reverence into the form is to miss the intimacy that is actually there.

The graver loss is interpretive. When every thou and every ye is rendered you, the English reader can no longer see what the Hebrew and Greek plainly show. He cannot tell that the Lord's promise to Peter in Luke 22:32 shifts between the plural and the singular within two verses, nor that the great commands of the Decalogue are singular and inescapable. Modern translators did not remove the distinction out of malice; they removed it because English usage had already died. But what died was a real instrument of exegesis, and the reader who keeps the Authorized Version keeps the instrument.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'attah (masculine) and 'att (feminine), the singular you; Greek su, the second person singular, with its emphatic use when the verb already carries the person; Saxon þu, the English ancestor.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'attah (H859) — thou, masculine singular; the form of address in every singular commandment of the Decalogue.
Hebrew 'att (H859) — thou, feminine singular; used of Israel as the wife of the LORD and of individual women.
Greek su (G4771) — thou; when written out rather than carried by the verb ending it is emphatic, as in Matthew 16:16.
Greek humeis (G5210) — ye, the plural counterpart; the contrast between the two is invisible in modern English.
Saxon þu — the Old English singular, cognate with Latin tu; the direct ancestor of the KJV form.
usage: Of the singular commandment binding each man alone: Thou shalt have no other gods before me (Exodus 20:3).
Of God summoning the individual sinner: Where art thou? (Genesis 3:9).
Of personal confession before Christ: Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God (Matthew 16:16).
scriptures: Exodus 20:3
Thou shalt have no other gods before me.
Genesis 3:9
And the LORD God called unto Adam, and said unto him, Where art thou?
Matthew 16:16
And Simon Peter answered and said, Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God.
Mark 14:37
And he cometh, and findeth them sleeping, and saith unto Peter, Simon, sleepest thou? couldest not thou watch one hour?

pos: pron. (second person singular, objective; rendering Hebrew suffix forms, Greek se and soi)
etymology: From Saxon þe, the oblique case of þu. Where thou does the acting, thee is acted upon or spoken to — the object of the verb and the object of the preposition. Modern English kept the distinction for he/him and she/her but lost it entirely in the second person.
biblical_def: Thee is thou in the objective case — the single person receiving the action rather than performing it. Scripture uses it wherever one person is the object of God's speech, God's gift, or God's dealing, and the effect is to make the transaction unmistakably personal. “Behold, the LORD thy God hath set the land before thee” (Deuteronomy 1:21) puts the inheritance in one man's view. When Christ prays for the sifted apostle He says, “But I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not” (Luke 22:32) — and the singular is the whole comfort of the verse, because Satan had asked for all of them but the Lord names one. To the woman at the well He says, “If thou knewest the gift of God, and who it is that saith to thee, Give me to drink” (John 4:10), and the entire encounter is conducted in the singular, one sinner to one Saviour. The grammar carries the doctrine: salvation is not administered to crowds but applied to persons. Where the Authorized Version writes thee, no reader may take shelter in the plural.
webster_summary: The objective case of thou; the single person addressed, considered as receiving the action of the verb or governed by a preposition. In Scripture it marks God's dealings as transacted with a particular person — the land set before thee, the prayer offered for thee.
webster_full: THEE, pron. [Sax. þe.] The objective case of thou; the person addressed, in the singular number.
2. It is used after a verb, as I love thee; and after a preposition, as unto thee, before thee, with thee.
3. In the solemn and scriptural style it is retained where common discourse has substituted you.
4. THEE, v.i. To thrive or prosper; obsolete except in the old phrase, well may thee.
5. In Scripture, I have prayed for thee, Luke 22; the LORD thy God hath set the land before thee, Deut. 1.
corruption_summary: Nothing has been done to thee except that it has been dropped, and with it the reader's ability to see when a promise is made to one man. The temptation it now exposes is the opposite of individualism: it is the habit of hearing every personal word of Scripture as a word to somebody else.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle needing recovery is the personal application of Scripture. When the English text says you everywhere, a congregation may hear the promises corporately and never once feel them land. The Authorized Version's thee will not permit that evasion: it hands the sentence to one person and waits. Reading with the old pronouns in view is a discipline of honesty — it forces the question of whether the reader has ever taken any word of God as spoken to himself.

There is a second and quieter misuse, which is to treat the archaic pronouns as decoration. Some who love the Authorized Version have imitated its forms without learning its grammar, sprinkling thee and thou into prayer at random and often in the wrong case — praying to God as thee where the sentence calls for thou. That is not reverence; it is costume. Either learn the cases and use them exactly, as the translators did, or pray in the plain English of the age. God is not honoured by grammar mistakes offered as piety.
roots_summary: Hebrew expresses the objective singular by pronominal suffixes attached to the verb or preposition (-ka masculine, -k feminine); Greek uses se for the accusative and soi for the dative; Saxon þe supplied the English form.
roots_lines: Hebrew suffix -ka — thee, masculine singular, attached to verbs and prepositions where English needs a separate word.
Hebrew suffix -k — thee, feminine singular; frequent where the LORD addresses Zion or Jerusalem as a woman.
Greek se (G4571) — thee, accusative singular; the direct object of the verb, as in I have prayed for thee.
Greek soi (G4671) — to thee, dative singular; the person to whom a thing is given or said.
Saxon þe — the Old English oblique form of þu, retained by the Authorized Version.
usage: Of an inheritance set before one man: the LORD thy God hath set the land before thee (Deuteronomy 1:21).
Of Christ's intercession for a named disciple: I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not (Luke 22:32).
Of the Saviour dealing with one sinner: who it is that saith to thee, Give me to drink (John 4:10).
scriptures: Deuteronomy 1:21
Behold, the LORD thy God hath set the land before thee: go up and possess it, as the LORD God of thy fathers hath said unto thee; fear not, neither be discouraged.
Luke 22:32
But I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not: and when thou art converted, strengthen thy brethren.
John 4:10
Jesus answered and said unto her, If thou knewest the gift of God, and who it is that saith to thee, Give me to drink; thou wouldest have asked of him, and he would have given thee living water.
Ezekiel 2:1
And he said unto me, Son of man, stand upon thy feet, and I will speak unto thee.

pos: pronominal adj. (second person singular possessive; rendering Hebrew suffix -ka, Greek sou)
etymology: A contraction of Saxon þin, the possessive of þu. Thy stands before a word beginning with a consonant, thine before a vowel or h — the same rule that governs a and an. The Authorized Version keeps the rule with great consistency.
biblical_def: Thy is the possessive of thou: what belongs to the one person addressed. It is the pronoun of the covenant formula, because covenant is always particular. “The LORD thy God” runs through Deuteronomy like a refrain, and the possessive is the point — He is not merely God, nor merely the God of the nation, but thy God, bound to this man by oath. The great commandment is built on it: “And thou shalt love the LORD thy God with all thine heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy might” (Deuteronomy 6:5), where the singular possessive is repeated three times so that no faculty may be exempted. The Lord's prayer opens by turning the possessive back toward God — “Hallowed be thy name” (Matthew 6:9) — teaching the worshipper to be jealous for what is God's before he asks for what is his own. And the shepherd psalm rests the whole of its comfort on two possessives: “thy rod and thy staff they comfort me” (Psalm 23:4). Take the singular away and the verse still consoles; keep it, and the reader knows the rod is held by One who is his.
webster_summary: The possessive of thou, used before a consonant; that which belongs to the one person addressed. In Scripture it is the pronoun of covenant — the LORD thy God, hallowed be thy name, thy rod and thy staff.
webster_full: THY, pronom. adj. [contracted from Sax. þin.] Of or belonging to thee; the possessive of thou.
2. It is placed before a noun beginning with a consonant; thine is used before a vowel or h.
3. It is used only in the singular, and in the solemn or scriptural style.
4. From the same root as thine and thee, all being cases or forms of the Saxon þu.
5. In Scripture, love the LORD thy God with all thine heart, Deut. 6; hallowed be thy name, Matt. 6.
corruption_summary: The possessive singular is not attacked; it is simply gone, and the covenant formula goes soft with it. What must be recovered is the confession that God is not merely God in general but God to this man in particular, by covenant and by name.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle needing recovery is the particularity of covenant. Deuteronomy does not say the God but the LORD thy God, and the difference is the difference between a doctrine held and a bond entered. The 1689 Confession follows Scripture here in describing God's condescension by covenant as the way any creature comes to enjoy Him as his own. When the English possessive dissolves into a pronoun that might mean one or many, the reader can still know the doctrine, but he has lost the place where the text was pressing it on him personally.

There is a live pastoral misuse worth naming, which the possessive itself rebukes. Much popular religion is happy to speak of my truth, my journey, and my God, as though the possessive ran only outward from the self and made God a personal accessory. Scripture's possessive runs the other way first. Before Israel is told to love thy God, the LORD has said I will be their God, and they shall be my people; the belonging is His act, not the worshipper's claim. The Lord's prayer keeps the order exactly: thy name, thy kingdom, thy will, and only afterward our bread.
roots_summary: Hebrew marks the singular possessive by the suffix -ka (masculine) or -k (feminine) on the noun; Greek uses the genitive sou; Saxon þin contracted to thy before consonants and stayed thine before vowels.
roots_lines: Hebrew suffix -ka — thy, masculine singular; as in 'eloheyka, thy God, the covenant formula of Deuteronomy.
Hebrew suffix -k — thy, feminine singular; used where the prophets address Zion or Jerusalem directly.
Greek sou (G4675) — of thee, thy; the genitive singular, as in hallowed be thy name.
Saxon þin — the Old English possessive, source of both thy and thine.
The consonant rule — thy before a consonant, thine before a vowel or h; Deuteronomy 6:5 shows both in one verse.
usage: Of the covenant formula binding God to one man: love the LORD thy God with all thine heart (Deuteronomy 6:5).
Of zeal for God's own honour before one's own needs: Hallowed be thy name (Matthew 6:9).
Of the shepherd's instruments of comfort: thy rod and thy staff they comfort me (Psalm 23:4).
scriptures: Deuteronomy 6:5
And thou shalt love the LORD thy God with all thine heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy might.
Matthew 6:9
After this manner therefore pray ye: Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name.
Psalm 23:4
Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil: for thou art with me; thy rod and thy staff they comfort me.
Psalm 119:93
I will never forget thy precepts: for with them thou hast quickened me.

pos: pronominal adj. and pron. (second person singular possessive; rendering Hebrew suffix -ka, Greek sos and sou)
etymology: From Saxon þin, the uncontracted possessive of þu. It serves two offices: before a vowel or h it does the work of thy (thine heart, thine eyes), and standing alone it is the absolute possessive (the kingdom is thine).
biblical_def: Thine is the fuller form of thy, and the Authorized Version employs it in two distinct ways. Before a word beginning with a vowel or with h it simply replaces thy for the sake of the ear: “with all thine heart”, “open, LORD, thine eyes”, “the work of thine hands”. Standing by itself, without a noun following, it is the absolute possessive — the form in which a worshipper renders everything back to God. Hezekiah spreads the Assyrian letter before the LORD and prays, “bow down thine ear, and hear: open, LORD, thine eyes, and see” (2 Kings 19:16), asking God to turn His own faculties toward a threat too large for Judah. Micah promises the LORD will destroy what Israel has made: “thou shalt no more worship the work of thine hands” (Micah 5:13) — the possessive convicting, because the idol belongs to the man who carved it. And Melchizedek blesses Abram by naming the enemies as God's business: “which hath delivered thine enemies into thy hand” (Genesis 14:20). The word is small and the doctrine large: what is thine is what will be answered for.
webster_summary: The possessive of thou, used before a vowel or h in place of thy, and used absolutely without a following noun. In Scripture it appears in the great phrases of devotion — thine heart, thine eyes, the work of thine hands.
webster_full: THINE, pronom. adj. [Sax. þin.] Thy; belonging to thee; the possessive of thou.
2. It is used before a word beginning with a vowel or with h, where thy would be harsh; as thine heart, thine eyes.
3. It is also used without a noun following, as the absolute possessive; as, the kingdom is thine.
4. In the older writers it stands where modern usage would require thy in every place.
5. In Scripture, bow down thine ear, and hear, 2 Kings 19; the work of thine hands, Micah 5.
corruption_summary: The form is obsolete rather than corrupted. What deserves recovering is the absolute possessive itself — the confession that the kingdom, the power, and the glory are God's and not the worshipper's, in an age fluent in speaking of what is mine.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle needing recovery is doxology — the act of handing everything back. The absolute possessive is the grammar of worship: it does not describe God, it surrenders to Him. David's prayer at the gathering for the temple runs on it, and the closing line of the Lord's prayer in the Authorized Version does the same. A reader who has never used the form still needs the act, and the act is harder than it sounds, because it requires naming out loud what one had quietly counted as one's own.

The nearer misuse is idolatry of exactly the kind Micah names. The prophet's sentence is deliberately cruel to the craftsman: the graven images will be cut off, and then thou shalt no more worship the work of thine hands. An idol is always a possession before it is a god; a man makes it, and then bows to what he made, so that the possessive and the worship contradict each other in a single sentence. Modern idols are less often carved than built — a career, a platform, a portfolio — but the grammar of the sin is unchanged, and so is the remedy, which is that God removes what we will not surrender.
roots_summary: Hebrew and Greek make no formal distinction answering to thy and thine; the split is an English one, governed by the sound of the following word. Hebrew suffixes -ka and -k, and Greek sou and sos, cover both.
roots_lines: Saxon þin — the uncontracted possessive of þu; thy is the worn-down form of this same word.
Greek sos (G4674) — thine, the possessive adjective used absolutely, as in thine is the kingdom.
Greek sou (G4675) — of thee; covers what English divides between thy and thine.
Hebrew suffix -ka (H859) — thy or thine, attached to the noun; the English choice between the two forms is euphonic only.
The euphonic rule — thine before a vowel or h, thy elsewhere; the same principle that gives English a and an.
usage: Of asking God to turn His own faculties toward a trouble: bow down thine ear, and hear (2 Kings 19:16).
Of idolatry convicted by the possessive: thou shalt no more worship the work of thine hands (Micah 5:13).
Of enemies given over by God rather than conquered by man: which hath delivered thine enemies into thy hand (Genesis 14:20).
scriptures: 2 Kings 19:16
LORD, bow down thine ear, and hear: open, LORD, thine eyes, and see: and hear the words of Sennacherib, which hath sent him to reproach the living God.
Micah 5:13
Thy graven images also will I cut off, and thy standing images out of the midst of thee; and thou shalt no more worship the work of thine hands.
Genesis 14:20
And blessed be the most high God, which hath delivered thine enemies into thy hand. And he gave him tithes of all.
Psalm 38:3
There is no soundness in my flesh because of thine anger; neither is there any rest in my bones because of my sin.

pos: pron. (second person plural, nominative; rendering Hebrew 'attem, Greek humeis)
etymology: From Saxon ge, the plural of þu. In the Authorized Version ye is the plural nominative and you the plural objective, exactly parallel to thou and thee in the singular. The four-way system is complete and the translators keep it.
biblical_def: Ye is the second person plural — more than one person addressed together — and it is the pronoun of the congregation, the covenant people, and the church. Where thou isolates, ye gathers. The serpent uses it to make the prohibition sound collective and therefore negotiable: “Ye shall not eat of it, neither shall ye touch it, lest ye die” (Genesis 3:3). Christ uses it to lay a single condition on all His hearers at once: “Except ye be converted, and become as little children, ye shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 18:3). Peter's sifting is the classic case of the two pronouns working together — Satan desired to have you, plural, all the apostles, but the Lord says “I have prayed for thee”, singular, for Peter alone. An English Bible that renders both as you makes that exchange invisible. The plural is not a lesser word than the singular. It is how Scripture addresses a people, and losing it costs the reader every place where a promise or a warning is corporate rather than individual.
webster_summary: The nominative plural of the second person; the pronoun by which more than one person is addressed. In Scripture it is the pronoun of the assembled people — the congregation warned, the disciples commissioned, the church exhorted together.
webster_full: YE, pron. [Sax. ge.] The nominative case of the second person plural; the plural of thou.
2. It is properly distinguished from you, which is the objective case; ye do, but I see you.
3. In common modern usage the distinction is lost, and you serves for both cases and both numbers.
4. It is retained in the solemn style and throughout the common version of the Scriptures.
5. In Scripture, Except ye be converted, Matt. 18; Ye shall not eat of it, Gen. 3.
corruption_summary: The collapse of ye into you hides every corporate address in Scripture, and it feeds a real error: the reading of promises made to the church as though they were made to the private individual, and of warnings given to a congregation as though they were meant for someone else in it.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle needing recovery is the corporate address of Scripture. A great many of the New Testament's most quoted assurances are plural: they are spoken to a church, and they are kept toward a church. Read as private guarantees to the individual believer they are made to promise things they never promised, and the reader is then disappointed by God for a debt God never contracted. The plural pronoun is a guard against that, and it is the first casualty of a translation that flattens the number.

The error runs in the other direction too. When a warning addressed to the whole assembly is heard as you in the vague modern sense, every hearer may quietly assign it to his neighbour. The apostolic letters are largely written to congregations, and their rebukes are congregational; the church that reads them corporately must repent corporately. Recovering the distinction is not antiquarianism. It is the difference between hearing Scripture as it was dictated and hearing a blurred version of it.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'attem (masculine plural) and 'atten (feminine plural); Greek humeis, the plural nominative, with humas and humin for the oblique cases; Saxon ge, the ancestor of ye.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'attem (H859) — ye, masculine plural; the address to Israel assembled at Sinai and at Shechem.
Hebrew 'atten (H859) — ye, feminine plural; rarer, used of the women of Israel and of the cities.
Greek humeis (G5210) — ye, nominative plural; emphatic when written out, as in ye are the salt of the earth.
Greek humas (G5209) — you, accusative plural; the form behind Satan's desire to have you in Luke 22:31.
Saxon ge — the Old English plural nominative; the Authorized Version keeps ye nominative and you objective throughout.
usage: Of the serpent making a singular prohibition sound collective: Ye shall not eat of it, neither shall ye touch it (Genesis 3:3).
Of one condition laid upon all hearers at once: Except ye be converted, and become as little children (Matthew 18:3).
Of a warning to the whole congregation: Kiss the Son, lest he be angry, and ye perish from the way (Psalm 2:12).
scriptures: Genesis 3:3
But of the fruit of the tree which is in the midst of the garden, God hath said, Ye shall not eat of it, neither shall ye touch it, lest ye die.
Matthew 18:3
And said, Verily I say unto you, Except ye be converted, and become as little children, ye shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven.
Psalm 2:12
Kiss the Son, lest he be angry, and ye perish from the way, when his wrath is kindled but a little. Blessed are all they that put their trust in him.
John 5:33
Ye sent unto John, and he bare witness unto the truth.

pos: pron. (second person singular reflexive; rendering Hebrew nephesh constructions, Greek seauton)
etymology: A compound of thy and self, answering to Greek seauton. It is used both reflexively, where the one addressed is also the object of his own action, and emphatically, to press a command back upon the person who gave it or heard it.
biblical_def: Thyself is the reflexive of thou: the single person turned back upon himself. It supplies the measure in the second great commandment — “thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself” (Leviticus 19:18, quoted by Christ in Matthew 22:39) — where the self is not the object of the command but its standard. Scripture assumes self-love as a fact and commands that the neighbour receive the same practical care already spent on one's own body and interests. The word also carries the sharp edge of self-examination. Paul tells the spiritual man to restore a fallen brother meekly, “considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted” (Galatians 6:1), so that the very act of correcting another is bounded by a look inward. And it can be a word of judgment: Isaiah says of apostate Judah that she “didst debase thyself even unto hell” (Isaiah 57:9), the reflexive making plain that the ruin was self-inflicted. Whether as measure, as caution, or as indictment, thyself refuses to let a man discuss the commandment as though he stood outside it.
webster_summary: The reflexive and emphatic form of thou; the one person addressed, considered as acting upon or regarding himself. In Scripture it supplies the measure of neighbour-love, the caution of the one who restores a brother, and the indictment of self-inflicted ruin.
webster_full: THYSELF, pron. [thy and self.] The reflexive pronoun of the second person singular; used when the person addressed is also the object of the action.
2. It is used emphatically, to distinguish the person addressed from all others; as, thou thyself hast said it.
3. It answers to the Greek seauton and the Latin te ipsum.
4. In the plural the corresponding form is yourselves.
5. In Scripture, thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself, Lev. 19; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted, Gal. 6.
corruption_summary: The second great commandment is regularly reversed into a command to love oneself first, as though as thyself were the duty rather than the ruler by which the duty is measured. Scripture never commands self-love; it presupposes it and redirects it outward.
corruption_paragraphs: The therapeutic reading of Leviticus 19:18 has become almost universal in popular religion: one cannot love one's neighbour, it is said, until one has first learned to love oneself, and the second table of the law is thereby made to wait upon a programme of self-acceptance. The grammar will not bear it. As thyself is a comparative clause, not an imperative; it names the standard already in operation. Every man feeds himself, clothes himself, defends himself, and excuses himself without being told to, and the commandment simply demands that the neighbour be treated with the same energy. To turn the measure into a prior duty is to invent a commandment God did not give and to postpone the one He did.

The Reformed tradition has been clear here. Calvin observes that men need no teacher in the art of self-love, which is why the law borrows it as a rule rather than commanding it as a virtue; the whole force of the precept is that we are to be as diligent for another as we are already, and without instruction, for ourselves. Galatians 6:1 shows the only self-regard Scripture actually enjoins, and it is not self-esteem but self-suspicion — considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted. The believer looks inward not to find worth to affirm but to find sin to watch.
roots_summary: Hebrew ordinarily expresses the reflexive by nephesh (soul, self) with a suffix, or by the reflexive stems of the verb; Greek uses seauton, a compound of sou and autos; English compounds thy with self.
roots_lines: Hebrew nephesh (H5315) — soul, life, self; with a suffix it does the work of the English reflexive in Leviticus 19:18.
Greek seauton (G4572) — thyself, accusative; the form in Matthew 22:39 and in the summons to deny oneself.
Greek autos (G846) — self, same; the intensive element compounded into all the Greek reflexives.
Hebrew hithpael stem — the reflexive conjugation, by which a verb turns its action back on the actor, as in Isaiah 57:9.
Saxon self — the intensive noun compounded with the possessive to form thyself, myself, and the rest.
usage: Of the standard by which neighbour-love is measured: thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself (Leviticus 19:18).
Of self-suspicion in the act of restoring another: considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted (Galatians 6:1).
Of ruin acknowledged as self-inflicted: didst debase thyself even unto hell (Isaiah 57:9).
scriptures: Leviticus 19:18
Thou shalt not avenge, nor bear any grudge against the children of thy people, but thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself: I am the LORD.
Galatians 5:14
For all the law is fulfilled in one word, even in this; Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself.
Galatians 6:1
Brethren, if a man be overtaken in a fault, ye which are spiritual, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted.
Isaiah 57:9
And thou wentest to the king with ointment, and didst increase thy perfumes, and didst send thy messengers far off, and didst debase thyself even unto hell.

pos: pron. (second person plural reflexive; rendering Greek heautous with plural reference)
etymology: A compound of your and selves, the plural counterpart of thyself. It marks an action that a company performs upon itself — gathering, guarding, judging, or humbling the whole body together.
biblical_def: Yourselves is the reflexive plural: what a people does to itself. Scripture uses it most often for corporate duties that no one can discharge on another's behalf. “Take heed to yourselves, that your heart be not deceived” (Deuteronomy 11:16) makes vigilance the business of the whole congregation, because apostasy in Israel never began with everyone at once but was never stopped by anyone alone. Zephaniah summons a doomed nation to assemble for repentance: “Gather yourselves together, yea, gather together, O nation not desired” (Zephaniah 2:1). Paul commands the Corinthian church to act as a body in discipline — “put away from among yourselves that wicked person” (1 Corinthians 5:13) — a plural imperative that forbids the congregation from leaving the matter to its officers or to God. And the apostle's word to the Thessalonians, “be at peace among yourselves” (1 Thessalonians 5:13), locates peace where it is actually made or lost, between the members. The reflexive plural is the grammar of congregational responsibility: the church is not merely acted upon by its shepherds, it acts upon itself under Christ.
webster_summary: The reflexive and emphatic form of ye and you; a company considered as acting upon itself. In Scripture it carries the duties a congregation owes to its own body — watchfulness, assembly for repentance, discipline, and peace among the members.
webster_full: YOURSELVES, pron. [your and selves.] The reflexive pronoun of the second person plural.
2. It is used when the persons addressed are also the objects of the action; as, examine yourselves.
3. It is used emphatically, to distinguish the persons addressed from all others; as, ye yourselves know.
4. The singular form is thyself; the plural was formerly yourselves in both the reflexive and the emphatic use.
5. In Scripture, Take heed to yourselves, Deut. 11; put away from among yourselves that wicked person, 1 Cor. 5.
corruption_summary: Congregational duties written in the reflexive plural are commonly handed off — discipline to the elders alone, watchfulness to the pastor, peacemaking to whoever is willing. The plural reflexive assigns the work to the body itself, and no office relieves the members of it.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle needing recovery is congregational responsibility. Local-church polity, as the 1689 Confession sets it out, gives real authority to the gathered congregation and not only to its officers; the plural imperatives of the epistles assume exactly that. When Paul writes put away from among yourselves, he is not instructing a board but a church, and a church that has never learned to act cannot obey. Recovering the force of these plurals is part of recovering a working congregationalism rather than a nominal one.

There is a corresponding failure at the other extreme, which is the congregation that acts on itself without its elders, turning church discipline into a majority mood. Scripture holds the two together: a plurality of elders leading, and a congregation that owns the decision. Be at peace among yourselves stands immediately after the command to esteem those who labour among you, and the order is deliberate. The reflexive plural is not a licence for the body to govern itself apart from the men Christ has set over it; it is the refusal to let those men carry alone what belongs to all.
roots_summary: Greek uses heautous, the plural reflexive, and sometimes the middle voice of the verb, to express what a company does to itself; Hebrew uses the reflexive stems and nephesh with plural suffixes; English compounds your with selves.
roots_lines: Greek heautous (G1438) — themselves or yourselves; the plural reflexive behind the congregational imperatives of the epistles.
Greek middle voice — a verb form in which the subject acts upon or for itself; often rendered by an English reflexive.
Hebrew hithpael stem — the reflexive conjugation, used in the summons of Zephaniah 2:1 to gather themselves.
Hebrew nephesh (H5315) — soul or self; with plural suffixes it renders take heed to yourselves.
Saxon selfe, plural selves — the intensive compounded with the possessive to form the English reflexive.
usage: Of corporate vigilance against apostasy: Take heed to yourselves, that your heart be not deceived (Deuteronomy 11:16).
Of a nation summoned to assemble for repentance: Gather yourselves together, yea, gather together (Zephaniah 2:1).
Of church discipline as the act of the whole body: put away from among yourselves that wicked person (1 Corinthians 5:13).

Zephaniah 2:1
Gather yourselves together, yea, gather together, O nation not desired;

But them that are without God judgeth. Therefore put away from among yourselves that wicked person.

pos: pron. (first person plural reflexive; rendering Greek heautous with first-person reference)
etymology: A compound of our and selves. It is the pronoun by which a company speaks of its own action upon itself, and in the epistles it becomes the apostolic word for what preachers must not do — preach themselves — and for what they gladly are: servants for Christ's sake.
biblical_def: Ourselves is the first person plural reflexive, and its most weighty use in Scripture is Paul's statement of what preaching is not. “For we preach not ourselves, but Christ Jesus the Lord; and ourselves your servants for Jesus' sake” (2 Corinthians 4:5). The word appears twice in one verse and points in opposite directions: the minister is not the message, and the minister is the servant. Both halves are needed, for a man who will not preach himself may still refuse to serve, and a man eager to serve may still contrive to be admired. The same pronoun marks the apostles' ordering of their labour — “we will give ourselves continually to prayer, and to the ministry of the word” (Acts 6:4) — a deliberate refusal of good work in order to keep the best. It marks the fruit of affliction: God comforts us “that we may be able to comfort them which are in any trouble, by the comfort wherewith we ourselves are comforted of God” (2 Corinthians 1:4), so that consolation received is consolation owed. And it marks apostolic restraint in ambition: “we stretch not ourselves beyond our measure” (2 Corinthians 10:14).
webster_summary: The reflexive and emphatic form of we; a company speaking of its own action upon itself. In Scripture it is Paul's word for the minister who must not be his own message, for the apostles giving themselves to prayer and the word, and for comfort received in order to be given away.
webster_full: OURSELVES, pron. [our and selves.] The reflexive pronoun of the first person plural.
2. It is used when the speakers are also the objects of the action; as, we deceive ourselves.
3. It is used emphatically, to distinguish the speakers from all others; as, we ourselves have heard him.
4. The singular form is myself; the reciprocal sense, one another, is distinct from the reflexive.
5. In Scripture, we preach not ourselves, but Christ Jesus the Lord, 2 Cor. 4; we will give ourselves continually to prayer, Acts 6.
corruption_summary: The pulpit that becomes a platform for the preacher is the standing corruption this pronoun rebukes. The modern minister is encouraged to build a personal brand, tell his own story, and be relatable; Paul's rule is that the man in the pulpit is a servant carrying a message that is not about him.
corruption_paragraphs: Personality-driven ministry is not a new sin, but the present machinery for it is new. Conferences, platforms, and the whole apparatus of the celebrity pastorate reward the man who is memorable rather than the man who is faithful, and the sermon full of the preacher's own anecdotes will always be more immediately pleasing than the sermon full of Christ. Paul's formula is exact and it is not anti-personal: he does not say we preach no one, but that we preach not ourselves, but Christ Jesus the Lord. The test is simple and searching — when the congregation goes home, whom do they admire?

The second half of the verse guards against the opposite error, a false modesty that hides from people. And ourselves your servants for Jesus' sake: the minister who refuses to be the message must still make himself available as the servant. Acts 6:4 shows the apostles ordering their own labour on this principle, declining even the good work of serving tables in order to give themselves to prayer and the ministry of the word. That was not aloofness; it was the discipline of a man who knows what he is for. Between self-display and self-protection stands the servant, spent on people and pointing away from himself.
roots_summary: Greek heautous serves for all the plural reflexives, the person being supplied by the context; Hebrew uses the reflexive stems and nephesh with plural suffixes; English compounds our with selves.
roots_lines: Greek heautous (G1438) — ourselves, yourselves, or themselves; the person is determined by the verb and the context.
Greek kerusso (G2784) — to herald or preach; the verb governed in 2 Corinthians 4:5 by the negative not ourselves.
Greek doulos (G1401) — a bondservant; the word Paul chooses for what the minister is toward the congregation.
Greek proskartereo (G4342) — to give oneself continually, to persevere in; the apostles' word for prayer and the ministry of the word.
Saxon ure and selfe — the possessive and the intensive compounded into the English reflexive.
usage: Of the minister who is not his own message: we preach not ourselves, but Christ Jesus the Lord (2 Corinthians 4:5).
Of labour deliberately ordered toward the best work: we will give ourselves continually to prayer (Acts 6:4).
Of comfort received in order to be given away: the comfort wherewith we ourselves are comforted of God (2 Corinthians 1:4).
scriptures: 2 Corinthians 4:5
For we preach not ourselves, but Christ Jesus the Lord; and ourselves your servants for Jesus' sake.
Acts 6:4
But we will give ourselves continually to prayer, and to the ministry of the word.
2 Corinthians 1:4
Who comforteth us in all our tribulation, that we may be able to comfort them which are in any trouble, by the comfort wherewith we ourselves are comforted of God.
2 Corinthians 10:14
For we stretch not ourselves beyond our measure, as though we reached not unto you: for we are come as far as to you also in preaching the gospel of Christ:

pos: pronominal adj. and pron. (first person singular possessive; rendering Hebrew suffix -i, Greek mou and emos)
etymology: From Saxon min, the possessive of ic, I. As with thy and thine, English divided the word by sound: my before a consonant, mine before a vowel or h, and mine standing alone as the absolute possessive.
biblical_def: Mine is the older and fuller form of my, used before a vowel or h and used absolutely without a noun. The Authorized Version's mine eyes, mine hand, mine heart, and mine enemies are not poetic flourishes but the ordinary application of an English rule. The word carries some of Scripture's most searching first-person confessions. “Rivers of waters run down mine eyes, because they keep not thy law” (Psalm 119:136) — grief for other men's sin, wept by one man. Abram refuses the king of Sodom's goods with an oath already sworn: “I have lift up mine hand unto the LORD” (Genesis 14:22), the raised hand being the gesture of the vow. Most solemn of all is the LORD's own use of the possessive in judgment: “I have forsaken mine house, I have left mine heritage; I have given the dearly beloved of my soul into the hand of her enemies” (Jeremiah 12:7). Four possessives in one verse, every one of them God's, and every one of them given up. The word measures what is owned, and therefore what it costs to surrender.
webster_summary: The possessive of I, used before a vowel or h in place of my, and used absolutely without a following noun. In Scripture it appears in the great first-person confessions — mine eyes, mine hand, mine heart — and in the LORD's own reckoning of what He gave up.
webster_full: MINE, pronom. adj. [Sax. min.] My; belonging to me; the possessive of the first person.
2. It is used before a word beginning with a vowel or with h, where my would be harsh; as mine eyes, mine hand.
3. It is used without a noun following, as the absolute possessive; as, the silver is mine, and the gold is mine.
4. MINE, n. A pit or excavation from which metals and minerals are taken; a distinct word, from the Celtic mein, ore.
5. In Scripture, Rivers of waters run down mine eyes, Psa. 119; I have forsaken mine house, Jer. 12.
corruption_summary: The possessive of the self is the one pronoun the age has no difficulty with. What Scripture supplies, and what is missing, is the corrective — the constant reminder that what a man calls mine he holds as a steward, and that the LORD says mine of the same things with a better title.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle needing recovery is stewardship. Scripture never treats ownership as absolute in the creature: the silver is mine, and the gold is mine, saith the LORD of hosts, and the land of Israel could not be sold in perpetuity because the LORD held the title. Every human mine is therefore a tenancy. This is not a rebuke of property, which the eighth commandment establishes and protects, but a rebuke of the sense that what I hold is answerable to no one.

Jeremiah 12:7 shows the possessive turned to its most painful use. The LORD calls the temple mine house, the nation mine heritage, and Judah the dearly beloved of my soul, and in the same breath forsakes, leaves, and gives them into the hand of enemies. The verse is unbearable precisely because of the possessives; judgment on a stranger costs nothing, and this cost everything. It is also the shadow of the cross, where the Father delivered up His own Son, and the language of Romans 8:32 deliberately echoes the same logic: He that spared not His own.
roots_summary: Hebrew marks the first person singular possessive by the suffix -i on the noun; Greek uses the genitive mou and the emphatic adjective emos; Saxon min gives English both my and mine.
roots_lines: Hebrew suffix -i — my or mine, first person singular, attached directly to the noun as in 'elohai, my God.
Greek mou (G3450) — of me, my; the ordinary genitive singular of the first person.
Greek emos (G1699) — mine, the emphatic possessive adjective; used when ownership is being asserted rather than assumed.
Saxon min — the Old English possessive of ic, source of both my and mine.
The euphonic rule — mine before a vowel or h, my elsewhere; the exact parallel of thy and thine.
usage: Of grief wept over other men's disobedience: Rivers of waters run down mine eyes (Psalm 119:136).
Of a vow already sworn with the lifted hand: I have lift up mine hand unto the LORD (Genesis 14:22).
Of the LORD giving up what He owns in judgment: I have forsaken mine house, I have left mine heritage (Jeremiah 12:7).
scriptures: Psalm 119:136
Rivers of waters run down mine eyes, because they keep not thy law.
Genesis 14:22
And Abram said to the king of Sodom, I have lift up mine hand unto the LORD, the most high God, the possessor of heaven and earth,
Jeremiah 12:7
I have forsaken mine house, I have left mine heritage; I have given the dearly beloved of my soul into the hand of her enemies.
Psalm 38:19
But mine enemies are lively, and they are strong: and they that hate me wrongfully are multiplied.

pos: pron. (universal relative; rendering Hebrew 'ish 'asher and kol constructions, Greek pas ho and hos an)
etymology: A compound of whoso and ever, strengthening the relative into a universal. It leaves the person unnamed and the class unbounded: whoever he may be, of whatever nation or condition, the sentence applies to him.
biblical_def: Whosoever is the universal relative, and it does two opposite kinds of work in Scripture with equal force. In the law it universalises the penalty: “Whosoever lieth with a beast shall surely be put to death” (Exodus 22:19), where no rank or circumstance exempts the offender. In the gospel it universalises the offer: “whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life” (John 3:16); “whosoever shall call upon the name of the Lord shall be saved” (Romans 10:13); “whosoever will, let him take the water of life freely” (Revelation 22:17). The word names no one and excludes no one. It does not teach that all will be saved, nor that men come to Christ of their own unaided will; it teaches that the invitation is addressed without qualification to every hearer, so that no sinner may plead that the gospel was not offered to him. The Reformed reading of these texts has always been this: the call goes out indiscriminately to all, and it is made effectual in the elect by the Spirit. Whosoever is the warrant on which any man may come.
webster_summary: Whatever person; any one without exception. In Scripture it universalises both the sentence of the law, from which no offender is exempt, and the offer of the gospel, from which no hearer is excluded.
webster_full: WHOSOEVER, pron. [who, so and ever.] Whatever person; any person whatever.
2. It is a compound relative, and includes both the antecedent and the relative; as, whosoever will, let him come.
3. It is emphatic, and excludes every exception of person, nation, rank or condition.
4. The corresponding forms are whatsoever of things, whomsoever in the objective, and wheresoever of place.
5. In Scripture, whosoever believeth in him should not perish, John 3; whosoever shall call upon the name of the Lord shall be saved, Rom. 10.
corruption_summary: Whosoever is pressed into two opposite errors: universalism, which reads the free offer as a promise that all shall in fact be saved, and a hyper-Calvinism which grows shy of preaching the offer freely at all. Scripture's own use rebukes both.
corruption_paragraphs: The universalist reading takes the breadth of the offer for the breadth of the outcome. But whosoever believeth is a conditional promise, and the same Gospel that says should not perish also says he that believeth not is condemned already. Scripture nowhere teaches that all people will eventually be saved; it teaches an eternal, conscious judgment for the unrepentant, and every text that widens the offer is set beside a text that narrows the number of those who take it. The free offer is not a prediction. It is a summons, and a summons implies the possibility of refusal and the guilt of refusing.

The opposite error is rarer but real. Where the doctrines of grace are held without warmth, some have grown reluctant to press the gospel indiscriminately, as though a free offer to all were inconsistent with a definite atonement for the elect. The Reformed confessions know no such inconsistency. The 1689 speaks of the gospel being freely offered to sinners, and the whole Puritan tradition preached it so — Bunyan on the jerusalem sinner, Flavel on the fountain opened. Christ's work is effectual for His people; the call is published to every creature; and it is precisely the whosoever that gives the awakened conscience its right to come. To mute it is to withhold the very warrant God has provided.
roots_summary: Hebrew builds the universal relative with kol (all, every) or with 'ish 'asher (the man who); Greek uses pas ho with a participle, or hos an with the subjunctive; English compounds who, so, and ever.
roots_lines: Hebrew kol (H3605) — all, every, the whole; the ordinary way of making a statute or promise universal.
Greek pas (G3956) — all, every; with the article and a participle it yields every one that believeth.
Greek hos an (G3739, G302) — whosoever; the relative with the particle of contingency, leaving the person indefinite.
Greek pisteuo (G4100) — to believe, to trust; the participle governed by whosoever in John 3:16.
Greek epikaleomai (G1941) — to call upon, to invoke; the verb of Romans 10:13 and of Acts 2:21.
usage: Of the law admitting no exemption: Whosoever lieth with a beast shall surely be put to death (Exodus 22:19).
Of the gospel offered without qualification: whosoever believeth in him should not perish (John 3:16).
Of the invitation closing the canon: whosoever will, let him take the water of life freely (Revelation 22:17).
